full_judgment:
3. It is alleged in the application that the detenu is a small businessman and a law abiding citizen. He was falsely implicated in an entry in the general diary of the Kotwali police station under entry No.1326 dated 19-10-93 and on the basis of this entry in the general diary he was taken into custody and sent to Dhaka Central Jail. Thereafter, an order of detention under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 was passed by the Government under the signature of a Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, directing him to be detained for a period of 120 days. The grounds of detention were duly served on the detenu. It is further alleged that the detention of the detenu on the basis of this order of the Government was challenged before this court in Criminal Misc. Case No.1730 of 1993. Rule was issued in the said case on the Government and after hearing the parties a Division Bench of this court found the detention of the detenu on the basis of the order passed by the Government on 6-11-93 as aforesaid illegal and without lawful authority and accordingly, directed release of the detenu by its judgment delivered on 29-11-93. It is alleged that after the aforesaid order was passed by a Division Bench of this court a fresh order was issued by the Government under the signature of the same Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, on 1-12-93 vide Memo No.3643 directing the detenu to be detained for another 120 days and the detenu was not at all released in compliance to the order of this court passed in Criminal Misc. Case No.1730 of 1993. It is also averred that the subsequent detention order was issued on the basis of the self same grounds as those of the previous order of detention dated 6-11-93 which was found to be illegal by this court in the above criminal Misc. case. 

 5. Mr. Alaluddin, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that the previous detention order was passed by the Government on 6-11-93 directing the detenu to be detained for a period of 120 days and this order of detention was found to be illegal and without lawful authority by a Division Bench of this court in Criminal Misc. case No.1730 of 1993, long before the expiry of the period of 120 days for which the detenu had been detained vide the order of the Government dated 6-11-93. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in the face of the above order of this court holding the entire period of detention of 120 days vide order of the Government dated 6-11-93 as illegal, the subsequent order of the Government dated 1-12-93 was clearly a malafide action and a colourable exercise of power. He further submits that the grounds taken by the detaining authority for the subsequent order of detention were exactly the same grounds as have been taken for the previous order of detention passed by the Government on 6-11-93. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also submits that the detaining authority has devised a novel way of ignoring the order of this court passed in Criminal Misc. case No.1730 of 1993, on 29-11-93. He has also submitted that the detention of the detenu on the basis of the impugned order of detention passed by the Government on 1-12-93 cannot, therefore, be sustained. 

 7. The facts alleged in the application by the petitioner have not been challenged and denied by the opposite parties. From the records also it appears that an order of detention directing the detenu to be detained for a period of 120 days was passed by the Government applying section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974, on 6-11-93 vide memo No. 3676. This order is at Annexure A to the original application. It further appears from the certified copy of the order in criminal Misc. Case No.1730 of 1993 as at Annexure-E to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner that this detention of the detenu vide the above order dated 6-11-93 was challenged in the said criminal Misc. case and on 29-11-93 i.e. during the subsistence of the order of detention passed by the Government on 6-11-93, the said order of detention and the detention of the detenu on the basis of the said order were found by a Division Bench of this court to be illegal and this court also directed release of the detenu. It further appears from the order of the Government as at Annexure Band also the averment of the petitioner in paragraph 5 of the application that instead of complying with the above order issued by this court the present impugned order was passed by the Government under the signature of selfsame officer on 1-12-93 directing the detenu to be detained for a period of 120 days. This averment has not been challenged or denied by the Government. It, therefore, appears that the subsequent order of detention which is impugned in this application was passed while the detenu was still in custody and as such, there was no reason for the detaining authority to hold that the detenu was likely to indulge in "prejudicial acts" as defined in section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Moreover, when this court held the detention of the detenu for the entire period of 120 days with effect from 6-11-93 passed by the Government vide memo No.3373 dated 6-11-93 illegal, no fresh order by the Government could render the said period of illegal detention legal. It appears to us that there was no reason for the detaining authority to pass the subsequent order of detention on 1-12-93 while the detenu was in custody under an order of detention passed by it on 6-11-93, and particularly so, when the said order of detention was held to be illegal by this court. It appears to us that recourse to the subsequent order of detention was adopted by the detaining authority as a crude device to avoid the order whereby this court directed release of the detenu vide this court's order dated 29-11-93 passed in Criminal Mise, case No.1730 of 1993. The subsequent order of detention was, therefore, a colorable exercise of power and not a bonafide exercise of power with which the detaining authority is vested by section 3 of the Special Powers Act, 1974, and was, therefore, absolutely mala fide. 

 9. Before we part with this case, we like to observe that Article 112 of the Constitution enjoins all authorities, executive and judicial, within the territory of Bangladesh to act in aid of the Supreme Court. It is, therefore, incumbent on every authority, executive and judicial, to act in aid of the Supreme Court and, therefore, to meticulously execute the orders passed by it. Unfortunately, in the present case, instead of complying with the aforesaid mandatory provision of the Constitution the detaining authority, we are constrained to observe, has contravened the above provision by refusing to release the detenu and thereby flouting the orders of this court.
